newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Tension mounts as Albania vote campaign nears end.
newsitem.headline: Tension mounts as Albania vote campaign nears end.

text.p: Tension rose on Friday, the last day of a bitterly-fought general election campaign in Albania, following gunfire at a rally held by President Sali Berisha and signs of increasing violence in the lawless south of the Balkan country.

At least eight people were wounded on Thursday night when shooting broke out during an address by Berisha to supporters of his Democratic Party in Lushnje, about 80 km (50 miles) south of the capital Tirana.
One foreign journalist at the rally said she saw at least eight people with injuries in the town hospital.
The Democratic Party blamed leftist extremists for opening fire on the crowd, the Albanian news agency ATA reported.

The Socialists, led by economist Fatos Nano, gathered for their closing rally in Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square. Berisha was due to speak to his supporters in the same place at around 6 p.m. (1700 GMT).
In Tirana, around 500 international observers and another 100 monitors from the United States began leaving the capital on Friday morning to travel to areas where they will watch the voting.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is supervising the election.

The operation is risky and many of the observers, which include 112 parliamentarians from 22 countries, will have armed escorts provided by the Italian-led multinational protection force deployed in the chaotic state after the breakdown of government control in March.
The snap election was called to restore some measure of stability in formerly communist Albania after the establishment in March of an interim unity government made up of 10 parties.

The vote is being held 13 months after Albania's third multi-party elections since the collapse of communism in 1990. International observers said the 1996 vote was subject to manipulation and voter intimidation.
Democrats won 122 of the 140 parliamentary seats then. Berisha maintained that the vote was conducted correctly and ignored demands from Washington and some European states to rerun it.

But when a number of high-risk pyramid investment schemes collapsed early this year, the Berisha government's grip on Albania began to slip away. Thousands of people lost what the government itself estimated was around $1.2 billion.
Much of the south of the poverty-stricken country remains outside the control of any political party and has become little more than the fiefdoms of warlords or battlegrounds for rival gangs.
One member of the European Parliament said if the elections did not work Albania could become the 'Medellin of Europe', a reference to a lawless area ruled by drug barons in Colombia.
Fresh gang violence erupted in the past few days in the Adriatic port of Vlore, focal point of the March rebellion. About 1,500 people have been killed since the unrest broke out.
Finance Minister Arben Malaj, a Socialist, was pinned down by the fighting in Vlore on Thursday. Italian troops evacuated civilians from a rally in a sports hall as gangs exchanged gunfire.
A correspondent in Vlore said on Friday the town was eerily quiet but tense. Most people were staying indoors.
The OSCE's special envoy, former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, told the Albanian people on Thursday that every effort would be made to ensure the vote passed off smoothly.
"The election on Sunday will be one of the most important political decisions that the Albanian people have to take," Vranitzky said in a live television interview in English.
